---
order: 5
unit: words
title: Word chains
summary: "A general word can stand in for a specific one the reader has already met: a kelpie becomes the dog, then the animal. Readers link them without being told, which keeps a text moving without repeating the same word. It only works if the specific word comes first."
language: maths
node: [AC9E6LA04 n2, AC9E6LA04 n3]
explainPicture: { ref: text.yml#explain-pic, caption: "The eagle comes first, then the bird and the hungry hunter. The rabbit comes first, then the little animal." }
hook: "'Grandpa bought a kelpie. The dog follows him everywhere.' The second sentence never says kelpie. How do you know it is the same animal?"
---
A text can talk about the same thing with different words. A **general** word (dog, animal, boat, place) can stand in for a **specific** one the reader met earlier (a kelpie called Biscuit, a red kayak, Hobart). Together these words make a **word chain**.

## Predict: is it the same thing?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to whether 'the vehicle' is the same as 'the tractor' shows students already link general and specific words without noticing."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "'Dad drove the tractor into the shed. The vehicle was covered in mud.' What is the vehicle?"
  options: ["The tractor", "A different vehicle in the shed", "The shed", "You can't tell"]
  actual: "The tractor. Vehicle is a general word, and the only vehicle the reader has met is the tractor, so the reader links them without being told."
```

## Try: colour the word chains

```step
stage: run
insight: "Colouring the specific and general words for the same thing makes a word chain visible, including words that look nothing alike."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#run", height: 330 }
hint: ["Chain 1 is every naming word or phrase for Biscuit. Chain 2 is every naming word or phrase for the sheep. Leave pointing words such as she and them alone.", "The dog and this clever animal are both Biscuit. The flock and the mob are both the sheep."]
smaller:
  check: { type: question, q: "Every morning, the dog rounds up the sheep. Which dog is it?", options: ["Biscuit, the kelpie", "A different dog", "You can't tell"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "Only one dog has been named so far.", "The only dog the reader has met is Biscuit."], explain: "The dog is a general word for Biscuit, the kelpie the reader already met." }
check: { type: board, text: "Colour two word chains: every naming word or phrase for Biscuit, and every one for the sheep (not she or them).", when: "chains_ok = 2 and n_stray = 0", explain: "Biscuit, a kelpie, the dog and this clever animal are one chain. Sheep, the flock and the mob are another. The words change but the thing doesn't." }
```

Were you right about the tractor? Here the dog and this clever animal worked the same way.

## Worked example: general for specific

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Modelling 'what specific thing could this general word mean?' gives the method. Nib's slip is using the general word before the specific one."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each specific word to a general word that could stand in for it later."
      pairs:
        - ["Granny Smiths", "apples"]
        - ["a kelpie", "the dog"]
        - ["Hobart", "the city"]
        - ["a hammer", "the tool"]
      explain: "Each general word names the group the specific one belongs to, so a reader can link them."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: "working.txt#nib"
      text: "Here is Nib's paragraph, one sentence per line. Click the first line where a general word comes before the reader knows what it stands for."
      answer: 1
      fault: logic
      misconception: general-before-specific
      explain: "Line 1: 'The vehicle' comes before the reader knows what it is. A reader can only link a general word to a specific one they have already met. Start with the minibus, then call it the vehicle."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Why do writers swap a specific word for a general one?"
      options: ["To keep talking about the same thing without repeating the same word", "To make the reader guess what it is", "Because specific words are less correct", "To start a new topic"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "A good word chain never makes the reader guess.", "Specific words are often better. The general one gives variety later.", "The general word stays on the same topic."]
      explain: "A word chain keeps the reader on the same thing with a little variety, as long as the specific word came first."
```

### Linking a general word

```worked
\text{Spot a general word} :: Look for a word for a group: dog, animal, vehicle, city, tool, team.
\text{Look back} :: Find the specific thing it could stand for: a kelpie, the tractor, Hobart.
\text{Check it's the only one} :: If two things could fit (two dogs), the reader can't tell. Use the name instead.
\text{Check the order} :: The specific word must come first, or the general word has nothing to link to.
```

Now match some specific words to the general words that could stand in for them.

## Vary: draw the link

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Tracing a general word back with an arrow joins this lesson to the pointing words from the warm-up: both point back."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#vary", height: 300 }
hint: ["Click the dotted words, then click what each one stands for.", "The boat is the red kayak. This small craft is the same kayak."]
check: { type: board, text: "Draw an arrow from each dotted general word back to the specific thing it stands for.", when: "n_right = 3 and n_wrong = 0", explain: "The boat and this small craft both point back to the red kayak, and the water points back to Lake Burley Griffin. General words point back just like it and they." }
```

## Practise: three chains

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Three chains mixing names, repeats, synonyms and general words make students use every kind of link from the unit."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#practise", height: 340 }
hint: ["The paragraph is about an engineer, a robot and the caves it explores. Use one chain for each.", "Dr Amira Hassan is the engineer. Kestrel, the rover and the machine are the robot. The tunnels are the caves."]
check: { type: board, text: "Colour three chains of naming words: the engineer, the robot and the caves.", when: "chains_ok = 3 and n_stray = 0", explain: "Dr Amira Hassan, the engineer and Hassan; Kestrel, a small robot, the rover and the machine; caves, the tunnels and these dark places. Each chain mixes a name, a general word and a repeat." }
```

## Make: your own chain

In your own document, write four sentences about a specific thing: your pet, a favourite place or a team. Name it first. Then use a general word for it at least once (the dog, the town, the team).

Then use the highlighter in your document. Colour the chain for your thing in one colour, and a second chain in another colour if you have one.

Here is one example: "**Ollie** is our **cat**. **The animal** sleeps on **the couch** all day. **That sofa** is covered in fur." *Ollie*, *cat* and *the animal* are one chain. *The couch* and *That sofa* are a second one.

Then swap with a partner. Does every general word come after the specific one it stands for? Could any of them be a different thing?

```step
stage: make
insight: "Writing a paragraph with a deliberate word chain, including a general word, is the node's production step."
hint: ["Choose one specific thing, such as your pet, a favourite place or a team, and name it in your first sentence.", "Use a general word for it later (the dog, the town, the team). Does the reader already know what it stands for?"]
check: { type: reflect, text: "I wrote four sentences with a specific word first and a general word after it, highlighted my chain, and a partner agreed each general word points back to the right thing." }
```

## In your own writing

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "Checking class writing for general words with nothing to link to applies the move where it counts."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In a piece of my own writing, I found a place where I repeated the same word too many times and swapped one for a general word or a word that means the same. I checked the specific word came first." }
```

```teacher
summary: Students learn that a general word (the dog, the animal, the boat) can
  stand in for a specific one the reader has already met, making a word chain
  that keeps a text moving without repeating the same word. They colour word
  chains, trace general words back with arrows, and build a word chain in their
  own paragraph.
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 10 min · Vary 6 min · Practise 6
  min · Make and own writing 10 min
goals:
  - I can find a general word that stands in for a specific one.
  - I can say what specific thing a general word points back to.
  - I can use a word chain in my own writing, with the specific word first.
struggle: "Students read straight past general-for-specific links because they
  feel natural. The arrow in Vary helps: a general word points back, just like
  it."
before: >
  Do the Try board yourself: Biscuit, a kelpie, the dog and this clever animal
  are one chain.


  The one idea: a general word can stand in for a specific one the reader
  already met. This is AC9E6LA04 node 2 (word associations: general for
  specific), a hinge for node 3 (using cohesive devices in their own writing),
  which the Make step covers. The Make step has no board: students write in
  their own document and highlight their chains, and a partner or you check
  them.


  "Word association" is the curriculum's term. "Word chain" works for students.
running:
  - "Predict: ask how students knew the vehicle was the tractor. Nobody told
    them."
  - "Try: ask why she and them aren't coloured. (They are pointing words, which
    are a different kind of link.)"
  - "Worked example: Nib's paragraph starts with the vehicle. Ask the class what
    they pictured before the minibus was named."
  - "Vary: link mode is back. General words point back just like it and they."
  - "Make: students write in their own document and highlight their chain.
    Partners check that each general word comes after the specific one."
stuck:
  - see: A student colours she and them in the chain.
    ask: Is she a word for the thing, or a word that points back to it?
    fix: "Leave pointing words uncoloured here: the chain is the naming words."
  - see: A student uses a general word that could mean two things.
    ask: If there are two dogs, which one is the dog?
    fix: Use the name where two things fit.
  - see: A student's general word comes first.
    ask: What did your reader picture when they met that word?
    fix: Name it specifically first, then use the general word.
stretch: Rewrite the Biscuit paragraph so it repeats Biscuit every time. Read
  both aloud. Which is better, and why?
support: "A list of general words: animal, dog, vehicle, place, city, tool,
  team, building, plant."
leads: >
  Next in Holding writing together: topic sentences that tell the reader what a
  paragraph is about.


  Word chains come back whenever students fix an unclear pointing word by naming
  the thing: the name joins the chain.
exit:
  q: "'We caught a flathead off the jetty. The fish was 40 centimetres long.' What
    does the fish link to, and why does it work?"
  a: The flathead. Fish is a general word for a flathead, and the flathead came
    first.
explain: >
  A **general** word can stand in for a **specific** one the reader has already
  met: a kelpie becomes **the dog**, then **the animal**.


  These words make a **word chain** that keeps the reader on the same thing
  without repeating the same word.


  It only works if the **specific word comes first**, and only one thing fits.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: How many different words can a text use for the same thing before the reader
      gets lost?
    prompts:
      - What helps the reader keep up?
      - When does a new word start to sound like a new thing?
    notes: As many as you like, if each new word clearly belongs to the thing
      already named. A word that could be something new (a second dog) breaks
      the chain.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: From specific to general
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Write a specific thing on the board, such as "a kookaburra". Ask the
        class for ever more general words for it (bird, animal, creature, it).
      notes: Each step up is a word a writer could use later in the chain.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: What did you picture?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Pairs read each other's Make paragraph aloud, stopping at each general
        word. The listener says what they picture.
      notes: If the listener pictures something else, the specific word may need to
        come earlier.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which word?
      type: question
      q: A paragraph starts 'The Sydney Opera House opened in 1973.' Which word could
        stand in for it later?
      options:
        - the building
        - the city
        - the harbour
        - the year
      answer: 0
      explain: The building is a general word for the Opera House. The city and the
        harbour are different things.
```

Last winter, [[the rover#b]] crawled deep into [[the tunnels#c]]. [[Hassan#a]] says [[the machine#b]] sends back photos of [[these dark places#c]] every day.
